review: Well, judging from the Steam description, they really marketed the game poorly. It's not an action-survival RPG, but a rogue-lite with open world and RPG elements. The gameplay cycle is to gather, craft better gear, loot bases, etc to defend your base daily from monsters. If you can't keep up that pace or are too far away before the monsters come, your base will be destroyed and its game over. You get permanent improvements for your character after your run. If they marketed this correctly, it would have been considered a pretty good rogue-lite. Instead they called it an action-survival RPG and all the people wanting the next Diablo are upset.
Dont buy if you cant play with a group, it is fun but not enough solo content

There's an abandon button right next to the exit button. If you happen to click that one by mistake it deletes your character and permabans you from the server so you can't even start over. What kind of psychopaths make that a feature?

First let me say that this is two very different and separate games.  Most of the reviews seem to concentrate on one or the other.

One is Terraria-like with these beautiful graphics, without the nightly attacks.  Your base is safe.  Nothing is coming for you.  You gather, upgrade your various crafting stations, build better stuff, then venture out further.  There are LOTS of content to keep you from getting bored.  That's Survival Mode.  

You can play that with up to 10 people, public, or with your friends only (password).  Imagine if your Terraria Saved file was on the game's server.  So anyone could play at any point, and you couldn't cheat and change the save file.

The other type is much more of an onslaught of enemies and then enormous enemies coming for your base.  Everything has been prebuilt, you go and upgrade stuff.


I was worried when I saw the reviews.  Noway would I get something less than 90% positive but a bff really wanted me to try it.   That was Friday.  It's Friday evening, and my partner, roommate, and friends and I have done nothing but play this constantly.  Loving it!!

Turns out most of the complaints have already been addressed in updates.  SO glad I bought this and several more for people in my circle.

Look forward to more content.

I have a bunch of hours with Tribes of Midgard and have thoroughly enjoyed my time playing the game. I cannot recommend this game though because of a baffling user experience decision made by the developers to put a functionally 'ban me forever' button right next to the 'safely save and quit' button. The correct button says 'Save and quit' while the danger button says 'Abandon world'. I wish I could say I was joking, it's been a problem in the game for years and the devs don't seem to care. Because of this button, one of our players is now unable to play with us, which is effectively preventing the entire group from playing. The button might as well have said 'uninstall' because now all 5 of us regret buying a game we can't play together.

And what makes it so perplexing is, why even have a ban me forever button? What purpose does it serve to the user experience? If you go through the reddit and the Discord comments about world abandoning, it's exclusively people complaining about this button existing and bricking their playthroughs. Even with the new update, the moderators is still telling people not to click it and explaining to people that yes, you clicked 'Abandon world' and you can never go back. Which makes me think the devs keep it there for their own sick enjoyment. You'd think this would have ideally not even ever been implemented or at least been fixed immediately after the first person uninstalled the game because they got banned from their own world.

If the devs can remove this button, and undo the perma bans, then the game will be playable. But as of right now this was a waste of money for me.

Update: As of 4/11/2023 an update came out which visually changes the 'Abandon World' button. I do not believe this issue has been fixed. I think the button should be moved to an overflow menu. There is a UX precedent for how to delete a save. Even if the intention is remove a player from a world for server space reason, allow them to rejoin with a new save. Obstinance is the only reason I can think of as to why this is still an issue.

This is a bizarre, bizarre case. The reason you're seeing this game everywhere, and the reason there are ANY positive reviews is that the ***design*** of this game is actually... weirdly brilliant. The ideas and gameplay loop/structure are a breakthrough that is genuinely ahead of their time. What's happened here is that a brilliant design team has been put in charge of making a game with what appears to be development entirely outsourced to Fiverr. Please don't buy this game. Let's not encourage this type of predatory business model on Steam.

If you look up the developer, "Norsfell Games" you'll find that they quickly purged their entire history from the internet when this game took off. However if you look hard enough, you'll find that they've existed since 2013, making standard money trap mobile games. Everything about this mess of a product has become clear after I finding this out.
Surprisingly, given their roots, the monetization model here is not a problem at all. There's microtransations, but they're (currently) totally inoffensive. The art (especially UI) also absolutely does have "that" look, but it doesn't matter. The real issue is that it's PAINFULLY obvious that this company has outsourced all art and development to one of those huge firms from Asia or Eastern Europe that churn out turn-and-burn mobile games as quickly as possible for companies in the western market.

The game is a janky, buggy mess. All of the movement, gathering, attack animations are clearly purchased stock that feel like placeholders in an alpha release. Combat is far from being fun in any way. The whole "fighting the jotun" thing we all saw videos of and wanted to buy the game for? Yeah that consists of standing at their feet tapping the attack button while occasionally rolling away from their three very, very slow attacks with completely random collision boxes. Genuinely the closest thing to applying skill or thoughtfulness is these fights is that to attack them, you have to be clipped inside their feet, and you build up an understanding for where their collision boxes are during various attack animations, so you can to roll out of their model without getting stuck.

There are several menus that break in the same way every time you interact with them. There are several ways to repeatably break your controls, softlocking the game for you. There is a "I'm stuck, kill me" button in the menu, and you will be pressing it often. No, it does not refund what you lose, and you still have to go back to where you were stuck to attempt get your gear.

First of all, the game is not bad! It is quite fun to play. It is innovative and motivates to go further and discover the world.

BUT: There is simply a lack of content. You usually finish the game after 6-8 hours and that for the current 20€. The biggest problem is that the current season rewards you with many items, but only if you play a lot and that is simply no fun, because you have already explored everything of the game very quickly. We absolutely adore this game. It's a great Viking-themed open-world survival game with farming, crafting, and killing NPCs. We are hooked but one thing is a huge turn-off for us: the building or construction limit (max # of tiles). 

I was shocked when the little NPC popped up and told me I had hit the construction limit. This means I could no longer place anything, including digging for essences. I barely built a small two-floor base (didn't even have the whole roof finished) and two small bases with shrines on other islands. This needs to be addressed -- I highly doubt with money and time invested there could be a better outcome. I read a few replies from the developers saying they increased the amount.. well, I hit it, and it's still not a lot. I hope something will be further done about this issue.

What is this game?
A top down view, WASD move, clicker with 3 abilites per weapon, and there are bows, shields, one handed swords, one handed axes, two handed hammers and runes which modify damage output and playstyles.

The abilities on weapons offer playstyles like healer, support, or pure damage and you dont have to pick either/or, just hit the one you want to cast out of the three.

This is a time management game, and it's session based (similar to playing  a game of starcraft where you build up and you have your build orders but when its over, its over and you do it again and again).

The above statement is not a critique, it is a really fun game and its VERY in-depth. Layers and layers of mechanics will be revealed to you as you master the game. Its easy to pickup and really rewards you for mastering it, because you will be SO MUCH BETTER at it than your peers if you do so.

Two modes: 
- SAGA (basically 14 days to kill 2 saga bosses, and kill around 5 Jotuns (giants) as they head to your base every 10 min after last one is killed) before it becomes eternal winter. Exit the session through the purple crystal structure (bifrost) to gain your rewards.
- Survival, unlimited days to kill only jotuns and much larger map sizes. So no saga bosses. This mode is for fun with friends in a more lasting way and to test different builds basically because the Jotuns gain health and damage every time they spawn, making possible very difficult health pools to deplete, so you'll need to figure out how to scale out damage into late game.

You get golden horns (a soft currency) for beating saga bosses (5x per kill) and for kill Jotuns(giants) 1x per kill. You spend these horns in game to make legendary gear, to gamble on powerful runes early game. You also spend them on unlocking the ability to craft the powerful armor and weapons (which will be unavailable to you when you first start).

So yes, while it is a session based game, you keep your "progression" through out all your sessions.

There are also several classes you can pick (AND UNLOCK!). It is truly a fun, game.

This game is weird. First of all, it's terribly unpolished in basically every way possible. It's not [i]broken[/i], but it feels just shy of being so.

I have only played the survival mode, but the pacing is horrible. At the start of the game you struggle a lot against the game mechanics (not even challenging enemies, just gameplay inconveniences), but then before you know you have every crafting station maxed out and there is basically nothing else to do.

There are 2 kinds of bosses: "Jotunn", which are early game bosses with very generic mechanics, whose drops unlock new crafting stations, and the other kind I forgot the name, which have more specialized mechanics that are genuinely fun, but placed so far into the game's material progression that you're really OP by the point you go fight them, so they end up being total pushovers.

In addition to the weird pacing, there are lots and lots of small frustrations mostly related to polish, or just badly thought out systems. If you want a viking survival game, get Valheim, if you want a lootfest top-down action game, download Path of Exile.

 - First of all, what rubs me the wrong way is how certain items are locked to the "battle pass" progression system, or have to be bought with soft-currency in the shop which also shows hard-currency ($$$) items. This game does not have nearly enough content to fill out a battle pass with fun rewards, so it really feels like a way to drag your face over the shop so you maybe buy something;
 - While I'm dissing the shop, it's not even a good shop. You can get item recipes at the shop, but those locked recipes still show up in-game, it just says "go to the shop to unlock", with no pricing information, along with the stats. But there is no way to open the shop in-game, you have to actually LOG OUT of your session and visit the shop from the main menu. However, the shop on the main menu has the price and the ability to buy, but does NOT show the stats! This means that an informed purchase requires entering a world to see the stats of the item you want, leave the world to go to the shop, see the price (possibly log into the game again to farm some currency), then buy it and log into the game again to actually craft the thing. If you want to force a shop mechanic onto the players, it should at least be convenient to use!
 - Again regarding the shop, this is a paid game with optional cosmetics using a paid intermediary currency. Just use the DLC feature on Steam and be upfront with the pricing! The main menu really feels like they meant to port this game to mobile.


Now to the actual game:

 - You can build bases, but that is literally useless, as they have no practical uses like keeping monsters away or whatever, it just makes reaching your crafting stations harder;
 - You can build bases with a roof or multiple floors, but the fade out effect is terrible, making navigating the lower floors very annoying. Since there is no gameplay benefit for having a roof, I just made a couple walls open to the sky to keep visibility.
 - In this game you build lots of different crafting stations, and you can upgrade them to higher levels using materials. However, breaking them does not yield all the materials you used to build them! So breaking a high-level crafting station means gathering more materials again, which means you don't want to move them if you don't have to.
 - Also, the building limit is very small. Using the roofless technique described above, I could only make two tiny houses, packed as tightly as possible, before reaching it. This is not a game where you would have a "forward base" or something like that.
 - Storage is kind of nice, it uses the same system as Terraria in that you can craft with items from nearby chests without having to pull items to your inventory. And while there is a "deposit all" button, there is not a "withdraw all" one, so moving your chest around as your base grows is very unwieldy, requiring clicking on each item (and there are [i]a lot[/i] of different item types in this game)
 - The physics in this game is horrible, not only monster attack hitboxes are terrible, but you get stuck in every kind of terrain that isn't a perfectly flat field of freshly mown grass.
 - Speaking of monster attacks, there are no wind-up animations, and the Jotunn bosses' attacks are not correspondent to their animations. The ice jotunn has 2 attacks with the same animation, the fire jotunn shoots projectiles out of any angle, even though the animation suggests he is spitting fire, the dark jotunn has a basically instakill AOE that is triggered in the span of half a second, so you always have to fight her with your eyes glued to your own character, so you can't see the boss's animations.
 - Skill descriptions are clearly handwritten, with outdated values that don't match anything you see on screen.
 - The game has "elemental damage types", and various different tiers of weapons. But not every weapon element goes up to the same tier at the end game (I ended up using a Dark bow against Dark enemies because it was a tier above the best Thunder bow, so even though it dealt reduced damage it was still more powerful than using the correct counter-element of a lower tier.)
 - Bows are super unbalanced, at the early game you are dealing maybe 20% of the damage a melee weapon does, but then they surge up insanely at the end game and there is no point of going melee, where you could actually (gasp!) get hit.
 - The map is huge, but is mostly made of boring filler content that gives shit rewards. A escalating series of enemy "encampments", but after the first couple upgrades, 80% of the map is trivially easy, and gives resources that only end up piling up in storage because you have no use for them.
 - There are lots of game mechanics you unlock towards the later game, but they are completely superfluous. Potions are useful for about 2 hours of gameplay between you unlocking them (and being able to afford crafting them!) and you not needing them anymore because you have armor that does the same thing or better, but permanent.
 - Food is terrible, it heals a tiny amount to the point I didn't even bother crafting it. You can only carry like 6 pieces of each, and each heal about 5% of your health after the early early game. There's also a cooldown so you end up being able to heal 30% of your health over... 2 minutes? Not amazing, just get the vampirism perk that heals on kill and murder the easy enemies (basically any of them).
 - Bosses get stronger every time you kill them, but it's just increased HP/armor, so it's not more of a challenge, just more of a bore. Most of them you can solo, just hold left click with a bow for 20 minutes until they die.
 - There is an "essence" system which is basically "planting" arbitrary resources (you can plant iron, not just plants, lol), and you can upgrade the rate these essences grow by playing a wave defense type minigame at certain spots on the map, but the essences are so unwieldy to use and the resources they offer are so abundant otherwise, there is no point in doing that except if you want to pad out time.

I guess the underlying theme here is the game is afraid of actually [b]challenge the player or ask them to think[/b]. There is grind, for sure, the bosses with tons of health, the sapling upgrades, collecting resources to upgrade crafting benches, but all those actions are a matter of time put into the game, not a demonstration of your mastery over the game mechanics. You find a new boss only for the items you get to completely trivialise the fight. You find a cold climate you have to bring cold clothing and potions to survive, but immediately you find a resource that allows you to craft a better armor that protects against cold AND heat better than the potion. There are elemental weaknesses but all the enemies are a cakewalk anyway so there is no point in caring, just get the best base damage and you'll be OK.
Decent game, if you have friends. Terrible if you are a loser with no friends, like me.

TL;DR this game feels like a very over ambitious, incomplete early access. It feels like the devs are scrambling to give purpose to much of the content they've managed to include in the game so far, while busily creating new seasonal content (i.e a boss) in an attempt to keep people playing and/or interested.  In my case, this hasn't worked.  I doubt very much I'll revist this game in future despite the first 15hrs or so being fun.

How can I thumbs up a game yet give it two stars?  The game isn't bad  per se but it's also not great, if I could give a neutral rating,  I would.  I believe the devs are actively working on new content etc, but as it stands there just isn't enough substance to make it worth full price.
 
Survival - OK so playing survival mode, this game was really fun at first. However the game ends very abruptly after killing the last boss, at which point the "end game" legendary gear is not even required.  This gear is not even craftable for the most part, due to being limited by season reward unlocks ,or purchasing with horns, both of which are incredibly prohibitive to the point even unlocking a full set to craft is near impossible.  These reward & horn unlocks also prevent the use of certain weapons with particular element types, so if at the start you make a fire bow, you can't upgrade that bow to TIII without unlocking the crafting schematic with horns.  Nearly all weapons are restricted in some way by this moronic feature which makes me wonder if this is in some way meant to act as some artificial way to slow progression.  Well it doesn't, you just work around it by making another weapon or element type, which is purely annoying more than anything.  So if I'm fighting an ice boss, I can't use a fire bow on it for eg unless I use an early game one or just choose another element or weapon type instead.  You don't unlock sufficient horns to unlock most of this stuff in one play through either, rendering nearly all of the items requiring unlocks completely pointless.  You basically have to chose do you want armour or weapon upgrades, because you can't have both and you most certainly cannot have an array of different elements for different situations.  

Base Building - great, you get all these building components you can unlock by upgrading crafting tables so that you can build said base. This base serves literally no purpose, none, nothing attacks the base so you can just leave all the crafting tables and storage chests out in the open (as I did).  It's all purely aesthetic but in consideration of how short the game is, I don't know why you'd even bother, even if you just enjoy building bases.

Saga - this mode is where the challenge & replay-ability of the game comes in.  Essentially it's a base defence however the base is generic and spawns on world creation.  You basically have limited time to upgrade your stuff while defending  the base against harder waves of enemies spawning with each day/night cycle.  My issue with saga mode, is that you cannot play multiplayer with friends on a world of your creation, you have to join matchmaking.  So I did a few solo saga runs which I did find fun, but quickly got bored not playing with friends so gave this the flick also.  This is where building a base would be awesome, but alas this feature was not used here.

Fun little game and I would recommend it at the $5.99 sale price. Progressing your character and building is not terrible. The game 100% feels like a mobile game on PC. Oddly enough you can only rotate your camera when in the build menu? One of the most bizarre things I've ever seen in a game.

Look y'all, i really wish this were an out of ten system, because i'm on the fence between yes or no, but since most people say yes i decided to go with no in the hopes more people would see this.

I'm going to give it to you straight, this is a game with a lot of good POTENTIAL. that is not to say in it's current form it is all bad... if that that were the case then i would've said it was a bad game and been done with it, but there are a plethora of issues from systems to tuning that make the experience decline very quickly.

so without further ado, here's my big list of Cons:
1: Multiplayer is both a semi-requirement and also dramatically reduces the individual quality. what i mean by this is: The game operates on a day night cycle where enemies spawn outside your base at night and try to enter so as to kill your dudes. you HAVE to defend at night, if you don't you'll lose on day 1 (although barely in that particular case). if you are alone, you are going to take hits to your tree (the defense objective) there's just not getting around it, that combined with the inability to gather night materials to make the better gear early enough for it to matter means that even if you are an absolute god amongst men, getting to fenrir (the current season boss, which is the last objective of the game itself for now) is a longshot at best, since you also have to do quests and kill jotuns and explore a huge map all while returning to base every 10 minutes to defend increasingly long nights that give you less and less time to do the above. now this is offset by multiplayer, but then the scaling gets shot to hell and resources to get that early momentum get warred over for the first 2 or so days of the game before the map has been explored enough for people to actually be spread out enough to get whatever resources are available to them (which usually also puts them in dangerous territory) 

2: The Scaling: so i mentioned it just a moment ago, but the scaling in this game is pretty shi-... bad. you begin each 3-4 hour play session (since that's about how long it takes to get to and then kill fenrir in games that do get that far) completely naked and with no tools or resources (until you get the quick start tokens, but i'll get there in a minute) such that you have to go around and gather basics off the floor to make your beginner stuff... however, the enemies in the initial area are so weak, you can actually just punch them to death with your fists, while naked, and down a reasonable number of them, enough to get a full set of armor and possibly even a free weapon drop. fast forward to literally zone 2 where all enemies (except goblins) have 12x the hp, hit you for 30-45% of your max hp even while fully armored, probably stun you, and have ranged attacks. simply put, things are either not a threat in this game due to gearing or scaling, or they're a case of no matter how geared you are, they will kill you almost instantly and in a way that is mechanically feelsbadman. and that's not even discussing the jotuns.

3: Jotuns: so every 2 or 3 days in game, a jotun(giant) spawns at the edge of the map and begins to very slowly walk towards your base. (when i say very slowly, i mean it will take them several days to do so) and the jotuns themselves are mechanically very simple, and for the most part choreograph their attacks, getting hit by their attacks usually means half your health if not instant death (which sorta makes sense, but is exacerbated by the next issue, which is perhaps my biggest anger point about the game)

4: Animation Locks: "Oh, the jotun just lifted their left leg, they're about to do an AoE stomp, better dodge roll out of the way so as to not die." *Character proceeds to continue swinging their axe 4 more times before the game realizes you stopped clicking 2 seconds ago* aaaand now you're dead.
For real though, the time it takes your characters attack animation to stop is so long, the enemies can actually start their attack after you, and finish it before you. it doesn't matter how much they show what they're about to do, there comes a point where you have to actually know the future in order to avoid being hit. this goes the same for blocking, but considering that shields don't actually do all that much to protect you in the first place, nobody wastes time trying to block attacks outside of the first game where they mistakenly think it might be viable.

5: Durability: Items have durability. like REALLY REALLY low durability. most classes have a means to extend the durability on certain pieces, but the amount of time it takes to unlock those nodes wastes so much time and so many points that you might as well just roll warden, which is basically the only class in the game that feels good on account of it being a pure utility class that undoes a lot of terrible feeling mechanics (like durability immunity) 
what really makes durability the worst thing to ever exist though is that, in order to repair an item, it requires a resource that is lost on death. i.e. if you die because your weapon broke, that weapon is now dead in the water, as you can no longer repair it. furthermore, you can't even partially repair an item, it's either pay the full cost to repair, or the item is broken forever. it's actually just bad game design.

6: Classes: i mentioned the warden above, but classes in this game can be divided into 3 categories: the classes that make you weaker for having them, the classes that are bad, and the warden. to begin with what warden brings to the table (and thus makes everything else completely inferior) it has no item durability (which on it's own makes it 200% better than the next best class), it's hearthstone (that's not what it's called, but the town teleport item) gets half the cooldown AND heals your to full and restores all your mana when you use it. they can build ramps to traverse difficult terrain FOR FREE, they can craft items for cheaper, they can literally resource dupe (on purpose, not as a bug) they have every weapon mastery, they can hold one extra rune (so 6 instead of 5) and basically they are the golden gods of this game that make it even possible to do all the things in a reasonable amount of time. following them is the Seer who's only perk is a healing aura and temperature immunity, following the seer is all the bad classes, following those are the 2 tank classes, which actively make you weaker on account of shields being worthless.

7: Fimbulwinter: as the days go on, the nights get longer, and the world gets colder. spend too long where it's cold and you freeze to death, simple mechanic you might think, however what makes it bad it that at day 14, it's only night-time forever now, and you'll freeze to death 2 steps outside the base unless you tryharded enough right out the gate to get full Utgard's armor (which grants so much cold resistance that you can basically go anywhere) or stockpiled infinite resources to make cold resistance potions forever (which only last 2 minutes for the cheap version, and 4 minutes for the expensive version, either way it's not a lot of time) however, assuming you DID make full utgards armor, you are now weak to fire, such that should the fire jotun be the level 3 or level 4 spawn, it will now be guaranteed to kill you with every attack, meaning that the world is now dead for you as there's no stopping it from killing your tree, since nobody else can go outside to fight it unless they are also decked out with full cold resist armor, which leads to the same problem. 

that might sound like a lot, but there's still a lot to like in this game, i just feel like those things don't really justify the glaring issues.
my recommendation is that, if you're going to play this game, play it with 3 other friends and not solo or quickmatch, since the tuning seems to favor this specific number of people.

But! There is a big fucking but. You can create local game sessions like in other decent projects. As an example, take a look at any game from Valve or Alien Swarm - a free game, supported by the pure enthusiasm of the developers, which gives you maximum freedom in how you play it, and by the way, you can also play it in 10th. And if before I could turn a blind eye to the problems of having to depend on the capacity of the developers' servers, now my friends and I have to wait 30-40 minutes or even several hours for a “spot” to open up so we can play. [h1]What exactly is Tribes of Midgard?[/h1]
To put it simply, the game is an ARPG roguelike with crafting and TD elements, and also unintentionally a speedrun on solo mode.

[h1]What do you need to do in order to "win?"[/h1]
Each game starts you off in a randomly generated, fairly large world. The primary objective of each game is to beat the final boss, but to get to that point, you will need to:

- Defend a tree located in your home village from attacks that primarily come at night (if your tree dies, it's game over)

- Kill giant sub-bosses (that spawn one at a time) that will begin a 2 in-game day march to your base from a random spawn point. If they get to your base unscathed, they will make quick work of your tree, resulting in a game over.

- Gather/forage for materials and currency (souls) around the map to upgrade your weapons and armor, base defenses, as well as to unlock access to the final boss

- Unlock access to the final boss before day 14, or an endless winter night begins where enemies will constantly spawn outside your base, making it harder to find time and sufficient players to beat the final boss.

[h1]Review[/h1]
Tribes of Midgard can be pretty addictive initially. Beating the boss requires experience and knowledge that is only achieved over time. With each failed run comes the desire to improve, with the end goal of finally achieving that first win. And no, it is extremely unlikely that any new player would ever beat the final boss on their first try, which is by design.

As others have said, this game isn't really meant to be played solo. Although it is by no means impossible, the time sensitivity of the game, large map, and long list of objectives to unlock the final boss, makes a solo run much more challenging, and unforgiving if your character dies. It can also be really tedious having to explore the map on your own and  with no real time to really "enjoy" the experience - you have to always be focused on your next objective in order to win on your own. This is why I called solo mode a speedrun.

Thus, the game becomes much more forgiving and enjoyable with friends; you don't have to be scrambling to explore the map and searching for your next objective all the time. 

And it goes without saying, winning in public random matches is entirely contingent on the knowledge and communication of other players. I don't think I've played any public matches yet that didn't have quitters, or players who kept dying every other minute.

To summarise, it is the drive to kill the final boss that makes this game addictive. Once you have killed it a few times however, gameplay can become somewhat mundane. I personally lost interest in playing solo once I killed the boss a couple of times. 
And while there is a survival mode without the endless winter mechanic, that's just it - a game, but without the endless winter mechanic. Not very interesting.

Thankfully, Tribes of Midgard has a great amount of potential thanks to its solid foundation, and the seasonal system works great. Developers need only add more classes, bosses, and equipment to introduce more variation to make this a great game for the long term, and I'm looking forward to seeing what comes next.

Tribes of Midgard has many problems. It's a promising, gorgeous game and can be fun, but at the moment it's buggy, frustrating, and extremely punishing. Overall, I'd suggest waiting for a few months and then checking back in to see where the game is at. For a more detailed look into the game;

Gameplay wise, Tribes of Midgard is very similar to Don't Starve - featuring day/night cycles, seasons, and resource gathering - with Diablo styled hack n' slash combat. 

Exploration is pretty satisfying. Biomes are diverse and interesting and the game captures a fun gameplay loop, although the first hour of every game is always slow and repetitive as players scramble to mine enough stone, wood, & ore to build a quarry. 

Combat is a basic hack and slash. Actions are queued up and most attacks animations are fairly lengthy, so dodging and blocking are massively unreliable, it's always more consistent to just eat hits and spam potions. At least, that's the case until enemies start one shotting you. Abilities are tied to weapons, with higher tier weapons having access to more abilities, and different weapons typically having different abilities with some overlap. 

Classes are honestly a joke. Warden and Seer are the two best by far largely for their quality of life and strong support abilities, Warrior is moderate for having extra mana to boost their most powerful attacks, and everything else is lackluster. Skill trees are also almost all filler - +10% damage with swords, +25% durability with shields, +20% thunder efficiency, etc. It's a total miss, as are the game's secondary build system, runes. You literally just run the strongest damage boosting ones you can find because they're random drops, otherwise you pick up ones that increase resource gain or provide hp regen. Many are borderline useless; increasing damage explosive jars deal by 50% when jars are already a bigger threat to you than to enemies, making you move 20% faster while overheating even though you should be circumventing overheating, exploding when you die, etc. This is the most rogue-like element we have, with runes functioning similar to items, but it's still not very close thanks to their rarity and 5 (or 6 on warden) rune cap per player.

Weaponry is wildly unbalanced. Bows are clunky, hammers are unwieldy, and shields are too slow to use. This leaves swords and axes which is what nearly everyone uses. There are also five damage types - physical, ice, fire, void, and thunder. Thunder is the best by far though - it does more damage to the creatures that attack your camp every night, the most dangerous of the Jotunns, and most generic bandits while very few enemies resist it - so everyone just uses thunder axes & swords. These weapons also generally scale better with the more powerful damage boosting runes anyway, so even less reason to try using off meta weapons.

Scaling is an issue. Every night you defend your base. In solo play, you can ignore this except for bloodmoons, and things are generally not too difficult. However, this game has a tradeoff; fewer people makes combat easier in exchange for increasing the amount of gathering that needs to be done by any individual person. In multiplayer, you have to fight tooth and nail to survive. Enemy hp & spawnrates scale with players, so night quickly becomes difficult with higher player counts, shaving away the limited time you have to complete the game. Jotunns also have scaling hp & armor, meaning by the 4th or 5th Jotunn in saga mode, they're going to take 10+ minutes of constant hitting to kill it. Also, they'll one shot you even with the best armor, so have fun with that.

Bugs abound. Interactions randomly getting stuck, WASD keys no longer working, block no longer working, items being unrepairable even with the correct amount of souls, invincible enemies, attack hitboxes that don't look like they'd hit but they do anyway, random pieces of geometry in the terrain like a tiny board on the ground hindering movement, maps not rendering, the list goes on. Many of these massively interrupt the flow of gameplay, and from my experience, I regularly see multiple of these every run.

Quality of life. Gear breaks quickly, and you'll need to stop mid boss fight multiple times to repair gear. Yggdrasil's health  slowly drains slows over time, for some reason. Enemies can hit you from off the screen, some of which attacks deal massive damage. You can't animation cancel your attacks, making dodging or blocking difficult if not impossible for faster attacks. Water instantly kills you, even if you can see it's literally only a few inches deep. Building is a clunky nightmare and everybody avoids using it at every chance they can. UI is clearly made for console, doesn't use space efficiently, lacks hotkeys, and has a painful ~0.5 second delay between inputs. Broken items won't be manually requipped after repairing them, even if the slot they fit into is empty. The Bifrost encourages players to bail on their team instead of fighting difficult battles. Achievements in the game encourage randoms to essentially grief by bailing from the game early, stealing from resource chests, etc. Do you see a pattern?

The game has plenty of issues to iron out. It's still a blast, but many of the design choices or lack thereof so far massively hinder the experience. It's a shame - this game has some very interesting boss designs, a gorgeous art style, and is genuinely fun when the game hits its stride. Unfortunately, it fumbles along the way.

I really don't understand the negative reviews of this game. I have owned the game since Season 1 and have played for almost 40 hours - most if it in Saga mode - without ever experiencing a bug that was notable, let alone game-breaking. Not saying they don't exist, or people's experiences are invalid, but it's just strange to me to see some calling it unplayable.

I also typically only play the game with 3-5 people, so have not attempted to max it out at 10 players. I could see where if the host was located far away or didn't have an excellent connection that it could be a problem. Also, not being able to join mid-match could potentially cause an issue if someone does experience a disconnect (not sure if they would be able to rejoin?), but again, these are not issues that are so prominent that they have affected me personally. I have played with people ~2,000 miles away without a problem.

From what I'm reading, it seems that some people potentially are not understanding the play-style, so perhaps I can shed some light on that for potential buyers.

[h3]What the game is [b]NOT[/b]...[/h3]
[b]A solo-player's dream game[/b]
It's obvious both by the name ([i]Tribes[/i] of Midgard) and the play style that this game is designed as a multiplayer game. I think it [i]could[/i] be fun to play solo (in Survival mode perhaps), but the game in general is tailored to, and will most definitely be more enjoyable for, groups of friends. If you are trying to solo Saga especially, it's just not going to be as fun in my opinion. I also don't think you will find yourself very happy playing with randoms as this game takes coordination and some level of trust among a tribe, and people can be ... well, people.

[b]Your next 1,000+ hour addiction (probably)[/b]
Tribes is also potentially not a game you are going to play for two months non-stop, but it's a game definitely worth returning to from time to time. My friends and I will usually play it intensely for a a week or so, kill the boss(es), complete some challenges, and then move on to different games and return when there is a new update/season. Perhaps there are people who play it more regularly and that's awesome! I think Survival mode tries to put in a bit more longevity as well.

[h3]Be prepared for a challenge![/h3]
I think it's important to note that if you are looking to play the "main" mode (the Saga mode) that it indeed [u]will be a challenge[/u] the first couple of times you play it. That's the point. You really aren't [i]supposed[/i] to get it on the first attempt, or even necessarily the fifth attempt, and it's supposed to feel a bit overwhelming until you figure things out and start to understand your priorities/goals. - You'll learn what's important, what's not, and will continue to progress further and further each run.

Your first couple attempts will likely only last a few game days (and thus be shorter games) until your tree collapses [spoiler]or you 'nope' out with the bifrost[/spoiler]. Once you start figuring things out and start getting closer to defeating the season boss, each run will take you just over two hours [b]maximum[/b] - because by that point you will likely be overwhelmed if you haven't already won, and eventually you may become skilled enough to do it in much less time.

Ultimately, when starting out and progressing, be prepared for around two hours of moderately-paced game play with basically "zero chill" while you explore, gather, gear, build, defend, and do other tasks to complete your Saga goal(s). Take your potty breaks in advance people.

[h3]Enjoy some chill game play in Survival[/h3]
The last thing I want to mention is the Survival mode because some friends and I just started playing this mode recently and so far I really enjoy it. I look forward to logging many additional hours in this mode and would definitely recommend it for those looking to experiment a bit more with various builds for gear and armor, master the structure building (like ramps), focus more on gathering and exploration, and just generally "exist" without the wild hustle and bustle of Saga.

Imagine if Diablo instituted a wave defense mode.  One could picture the village of Tristram needing to be defended against cyclical, ever more difficult waves of demons, with the objective being to see how many waves the village could survive under your protection.  Periodically, Diablo himself would spawn in some far-flung corner of the map to advance towards and eventually attack alongside those waves.  To add to that base game, tack on a resource gathering/gear crafting/structure building/town upgrading scramble into the mix, the ability to play with up to 9 friends or strangers, and you have the highlights of the hypothetical Diablo Town Defense that Tribes of Midgard wants to be.

Now imagine the whole thing goes to hell, but not in the way one would hope for in a Diablo game.  In Tribes, the combat is basic, tedious, and dull, consisting of animation-locked click attacks and special attacks that build up over time.  The UI is cluttered, poorly explained, and glitchy/laggy.  The resource gathering and construction mode are haphazard, time-wasting distractions that add complexity without truly enriching the experience. The town upgrades are expensive and reliant upon the aforementioned lackluster resource gathering.  The boss fights are infuriating: mindlessly repetitive damage sponges, even when they aren't curbstomp-difficult.

All in all, Tribes of Midgard feels like it's trying to be too many things, and not doing any of them particularly well.  In each session, the early game emulates the survival crafting genre, having you pick up resources off the ground before upgrading to gathering tools.  Late game, Tribes borrows the node-based resource trickles as seen in RTS games such as Dawn of War, if you can be bothered to manually find the resources needed to repair those dilapidated nodes on the map.  All the while, you play from a fixed third-person isometric perspective reminiscent of better hack & slash games, without offering the tactical nuance and interesting loot that makes those games engaging.  Finally, session play stretches on for hours, meaning its a serious time investment with little in the way of reward or enjoyment to be had.

I'm trying really hard to like this game, but it's just not sticking with me. My major issues are:

1. Saga mode feels like you're trying to speedrun a game. If you load into the map, explore for a little bit and don't find the biome you need, it's better to just reset your map than to explore and find it. Additionally, dying after spending 15-20 minutes gathering souls can just kill a run.

2. Combat feels clunky. The delay after swing/shooting your weapon feels weird, not sure how better to describe it. Rolling/Dodging, doesn't actually dodge attacks, that's only a skill for the Warrior class. With how slow you are after rolling to get back up to full speed, I've learnt it's better to just run and strafe enemy attacks. Bows are extremely underpowered. A T4 Light bow will deal only a quarter of the damage of the T3 Hesir sword.

3. The early gameplay loop is the exact same. Scavenging for resources, upgrading your village, etc. It's not entirely bad, but doing the same thing every single time you play really starts to wear you down.

4. Matchmaking and multiplayer. Matchmaking is pretty bad at the moment. My friend and I playing together will get matched with someone and have very high ping. Players can't join midgame and when you get a leaver you feel it. Mobs in multiplayer also have far too much health in the early game. We've noticed that with just two people mobs have twice as much HP. One could argue this is fine, but resources are not doubled so pacing gets staggered a bit and if one person doesn't pull their weight for a little bit, the group starts to feel it.

What I do like about the game:

1. The concept is amazing. Dropping into a randomly generated map, scavenging for resources, and building up a base is fun. I hope the construction side of the game adds to this, there is a ton of potential here.

2. Heroes are vastly different which gives a great sense of individuality. There does need to be some tuning done, but unlocking and playing a new class feels rewarding.

3. The art style and music are great. With how much time each run takes, it doesn't feel bland and worn out to listen to, even after a few hours.

Overall, this game has a ton of great potential, but the gameplay loop is starting to wear me down and with how punishing the game can be at times, it has me in a much more hardcore mindset which is just what I don't want this early in a game.

At 6 hours of game play, my profile is only Valhalla Level 5, and I have already completely broken the local ecosystem.

If you're coming from Valheim, your muscle memory makes this game an absolute power fantasy. The game tries to tell a serious story about a desperate Viking apocalypse, but the open-world sandbox mechanics are wonderfully exploitable:

The Real Estate: I bypassed hours of progression because the map generator gave me an idyllic woodland clearing directly over a late-game beach packed with passive seals, crabs, and high-tier gemstones.

Is it balanced? Not even a little bit. Is it fun to play? 100%. If you want a chaotic, rewarding sandbox where your actual gaming skill lets you completely bypass the progression curve, this is a masterpiece. 10/10 retirement home.

​I really wanted to love this game. The art style is charming, the Norse aesthetic looked promising, and the idea of combining action-RPG combat with survival mechanics sounded like a great loop. Unfortunately, it suffers from a severe identity crisis that ultimately makes it more tedious than fun.

The core issue is how the game dictates your pacing. It markets itself as a co-op survival and exploration game, but forces you onto a relentless, high-stress clock thats just way too fast. You are constantly rushing to gather materials, defending your base from night attacks, and hunt down Jotunn, leaving almost zero room to actually explore or enjoy the world at your own pace. This strict time pressure completely kills off creative or non-meta playstyles, funneling every run into the exact same routine, making it repetitive in an unfun way.

The combat felt really shallow to me. The animations felt really clunky & unresponsive "most of the time". The Base building and crafting systems feel like an afterthought. Placement mechanics are frustrating and inventory management was overly complicated. 

As it stands, it’s a repetitive loop that values artificial time pressure over actual engagement.

Some the bad reviews are mostly  due to people not understanding the core mechanics of this game and buying it on sale. THIS IS A SURVIVAL  ROGUE-LITE!! You start with nothing and see how far you can go before you lose. That's right, your world ends when you lose. 

For those who didn't bother reading the detailed guide in the game description before buying, there are two modes:

Saga, session based start from scratch and try to kill the Ancient Saga bosses as quickly as possible. Things to consider in this mode.
- you must defend the World Tree of life Yggdrasil or you lose and your Run is over and are unable to claim your rewards( Golden Horns)
-Every night your base is being assaulted by an onslaught of enemies, you must upgrade your base defenses, crafting NPCs and resource farms to get far
- There are mini-bosses Jotnar that spawn every two days and get harder the longer the days go. They have one goal, destroy your tree ending your run.
- 8 unique classes to choose from, with a level cap of 10 and no respect( as of this review)  so choose wisely
-Main goal is complete a set number of challenges, the main ones being killing all the Saga Ancient bosses. Each boss rewards a set amount of golden horns ( special currency for recipes, cosmetics and unlockables)
-Day limit, pay attention to number of days. Jotnar spawns every two days unless you haven't killed the last one. They get stronger and scale to the number of days at time of spawn. They take two days to reach your base and can obliterate it without you being there to defend within roughly two minutes or less if you left a gate open. 
-the map slowly approaches winter, at day 15 you can die outside of your base due to cold without proper gear
- after day 14 it is endless night, enemies will being constantly attacking your base until Winter ends
- Winter does end at day  20 but you probably die before that. So day 14 is your hard cap of time to extract through the Bi-frost and claim your hard earn Golden Horns
- While playing saga you need to make a list of objectives, gear/ weapons( no dismantling, you are stuck with whatever item you crafted) , what to explore, what challenges to complete, who to kill and time frame( 14 days or less) and when to leave before its too late. 

Survival Mode( weenie hut Jr. mode) 
- typical go at your own pace, chill building and exploration
-you can earn battle pass exp here too, but its slower
-less harsh than Saga mode
- lvl 50 cap with access to all blessings across all classes
- no need to defend base
-earn golden horns but much slower 
-no time limit or fear of endless winter/night

The battle Pass: its free, you unlock new recipes for your in-game crater, new load-outs and cosmetics to help you succeed. You premium currency for free cosmetics. You earn free golden horns. All you need to do is play and you will earn them. The pass last 6 months. If you miss something from old passes they can be bought with golden horns which you earn anyway. 

Why play this game? Its for survival enthuses that love a challenge and not afraid to die doing it. You enjoyed  playing dark souls on the highest difficulty and try to speed run it. You like theory crafting character builds. You want an ending to a survival game or a goal to work towards instead of just building the badass "blank" 

Are there bugs? Well I've been lucky and have experienced one bug in the 60 + hour of play time and that's missing particle effects( like invisible fire or attacks). This will vary from player to player. 

My only gripe is that its always winter, so you need to always be building towards a single armor set to prevent ice weather effect. Wish it was randomized weather effects instead of only winter.

A gem in the rough. I like the survival mode gameplay and mechanics and there is so much potential in this game, although I have several points to criticize:

- reduce grind: e.g. farming stone is tedious. There are so many boulders and rocks everywhere, but you can only mine rock at these small stone deposits. I don't want to run around mining so much rock... The crafting system needs some more balancing! Maybe even create hot spots for some resources, e.g. a large accumulation of rocks where one could place a portal shrine to quickly travel to for some quick mining, or a larger school of fish. You get the idea: something that is worth revisiting for specific resources.

- better balancing concerning combat difficulty: beating the first Jötunn was tough, beating the second one was easier, and after that I had zero problems surviving which kinda made fighting pointless except for the grind. Having to fight a bit more strategically to beat strong enemies or hordes would make it way more interesting. Currently I only have to spam two buttons to win. 

- remove "pay to win": I understand the appeal behind an in-game shop, and I support it -- if its only purpose is to support the devs via cosmetics, skins and so on. But here is a classic example of useful items (e.g. a fire-resistant armor) that is locked in a shop that you have to use a shop currency for -- which you can only get via excessive grinding or via spending real money. Unlock the useful stuff and put only cosmetics in the in-game shop, please!

- I can buy maps for locations that do not exist. E.g. I've been searching for another lair, so I bought a lair map from a sorcerer, but no new lair location appeared on my map. After that I learned that I already found all possible locations, which means that I uselessly spent my souls for nothing. There should be an internal limiter/indicator that prevents (or at least warns) dumb players like me from doing that. 

- roaming around the world is sometimes extremely tedious and frustrating because of walls/cliffs. A possibility to climb walls or build stairs or ladders would be such a relief. 

- the inventory menu is finicky. For example, unequipping or equipping runes always puts the "cursor" (playing with gamepad, so I'm talking about the currently selected item) back to the beginning of the list, or sometimes even to a random place. And if I have five runes that are at the end of the list and should be all unequipped, that means a lot of cursor movement...

What I like: the Jötunns also level up with every time you beat them, providing an end-game activity. The combat is straightforward. I also like the art style, and the maps looks nice. Worlds could be a bit bigger, but it's not overwhelmingly large, so that's fine.

We bought this game with a group of 6 people for our annual LAN. We were specifically looking for cheap, easy to learn, coop/ PVE style games. We really enjoyed the Genre of RPG Tower Defense (like Dungeon Defenders or the good old WC3 mods), so we went for Tribes and Midgard - and got exactly what we were looking for. This game does not require any skill whatsoever. You'll learn what your class can do, which weapon to use and strengths & weaknesses of the bosses during your first run. And without looking up strategies online, you'll need like 3-4 runs before figuring out how to beat the first boss easily (if you are an experienced group, maybe earlier). After that, the game lacks another level of challenge, as the other bosses are quite similar once you know what to do in Midgard.

Positive:
- easy accessible: this game is cheap (in sale!) and you can play it on any kind of computer, so even your reallife friends with their office laptops will be able to join your party.
- easy to learn: no depth means you'll learn this game in no time and even the noobiest reallife mate will be able to have fun and feel like he is contributing to beating the game.
- fun game mode: it's the classic "gather a group of friends and beat the evil boss while hordes of monsters try to destroy your base" type of game and those just always work.
- classic theme: while going with the frequently used theme of nordic mythology isn't that creative, it is still fun to choose your favorite class, craft medival weapons and beat up monsters 

Negative:
- as mentioned, this game has no depth. Once you know how to reach and beat the bosses, you'll never have a hard time doing so again. Also, lots of stuff added to the game (items, food, many weapons) are not at all necessary to win.
- few updates: we played the game in March/ April and recently looked what's changed til then - not one single update in almost a year.
-graphics, gameplay, UI... this game feels more like a mobile game than a title you'd be willing to pay 20€ for.

Do I recommend it? Not to everyone. If you wanna dive deep into a world, if you are looking for solo player action, if you have an expensive rig you wanna use to the limit or if you wanna challenge yourself - this game is not for you.
But if you have a group of friends that is not necessarily great at videogames, but wants to spend an hour or five having fun with friends while during holiday season, you will not regret spending 6-7€ for a game like this.

Tribes of Midgard is completely worth getting. I have almost 90 hours of active game time. Tribes has a lot of replayablility, each saga game taking from an hour to around 3 or 4 depending on your goals, luck, and skills. There are also 8 different classes you can try out which add some freshness to each run. 

The game does have a few cons, as all games do. First off, the matchmaking isn't the greatest. Not the game itself, but the people in it. The majority of your players will be either new players or just looking for some quick horns or exp. Players in matchmaking also won't bother to share resources as there's probably someone else who would take everything out of the communal chest. Basically, there's little to no coordination and all the enemies are scaled to the players making it very hard to solo which causes most games to fail quickly. The game also has a decent amount of bugs and a few balancing issues, but it's just been release and is to be expected.

Some things I would like to see would be a way to get platinum coins from playing games, of course only in small amounts, and a better way to get runes. It is very difficult to get the runes you want especially when you unlock the majority of them and add them to the drop pool. You CAN buy them with horns from the alter at base, but there should be some other method of purchasing them using a high amount of souls, the in game currency. Lastly, I think there should be some changes with the water mechanics. You can kill gods, but can't cross a 2 in deep river? A large portion of starting deaths come from just that.

All in all, the game is worth the time and money considering the devs are still working on updates so many things are going to be fixed as well as new things will be added to increase play time. If you're having trouble with the matchmaking and can't or don't want to solo, consider joining the Tribes of Midgard official server. There are a lot of people looking for a group and the community is coordinated and accepting to all players.
